title: Definitions Contain Limited Information
author: Matthew Evans
summary: Matthew Evans argues that asking students to define a term is one of the weakest ways to assess conceptual understanding, because a correct definition can be produced by rote and reveals nothing about whether a student recognises a concept's boundaries or can distinguish it from a near non-example. Using worked examples on osmosis and metaphor, he shows how a technically correct definition can mask a student's inability to generalise or to distinguish a concept from a confusable near-neighbour (metaphor versus simile). He then proposes five richer question types -- contrast, sorting, multiple-choice on defining features, extraction, and correction -- each designed to generate more informationally rich answers about the boundaries and application of a concept, while acknowledging no single question type is perfect.
points: Evans' central diagnostic claim is that definition questions are informationally poor for two reasons: rote-learned definitions can mask zero understanding, and even a correct definition-plus-example doesn't reveal whether a student grasps a concept's boundaries.

The osmosis and metaphor examples are the piece's sharpest illustration: a technically "full marks" answer can coexist with a student's inability to generalise the concept to a new context or to distinguish it from a confusable near-neighbour.

His five alternative question types (contrast, sorting, multiple-choice on features, extraction, correction) are each aimed at forcing students to apply a concept's boundary conditions rather than reproduce a memorised string of words.
Evans is explicit that no question type is perfect -- the point is deciding what insight is most valuable and designing toward it, not finding one universally superior format.
quotes: It is not unusual for tests to ask students to define a term or concept. However, these type of questions tend to generate informationally poor responses.
We do not know whether the student just learnt the definition by rote, with no real understanding of the concept.
A definition does not reveal anything about whether they understand the boundaries of a concept or what would count as a non-example.
It doesn't take an English teacher to know that metaphors and similes are often confused. The student's answer tells us nothing about whether this common 'non-example' is understood.
Asking students to compare things helps tease out whether they understand the core tenets of a concept and where the boundaries are.
None of the above questions are perfect, but then there is no such thing as a perfect assessment question.
